title: Prenatal organochlorine and methylmercury exposure and memory and learning in school-age children in communities near the New Bedford Harbor Superfund site, Massachusetts.
ehr_evidence: A sample of 788 mother–infant pairs were recruited from St. Luke’s Hospital in New Bedford, Massachusetts, at the time of the infant’s birth, between 1993 and 1998.
summary: Prospective birth cohort study evaluating associations between low-level prenatal exposure to PCBs, DDE, and methylmercury and childhood memory and learning at age 8.
key_findings: Each 1 μg/g increase in maternal hair Hg was associated with decrements of –2.8 on Visual Memory (95% CI: –5.0, –0.6, p = 0.01), –2.2 on Learning (95% CI: –4.6, 0.2, p = 0.08), and –1.7 on Verbal Memory (95% CI: –3.9, 0.6, p = 0.14).
No significant adverse associations were found for ∑PCB4, dioxin-like PCBs, or DDE with WRAML indices.
After excluding three high-exposure outliers, the adjusted estimate for DDE and Learning Index was essentially null.
captured_features: Cord serum PCB and DDE levels
WRAML indices (Visual Memory, Verbal Memory, Learning)
population: 393 children aged 7–11 years (mean 8.1) born 1993–1998 to mothers residing near New Bedford Harbor, Massachusetts
limitations: Low statistical power for PCB associations at low exposure levels
Hair mercury may be less sensitive than blood biomarkers
Missing data for covariates and exposures
Potential selection bias as included children had higher maternal IQ and education
Cross-sectional assessment of neurodevelopment at a single time point
